unit.title: Volume, surface area and symmetry
unit.blurb: Volume of prisms and cylinders, surface area of triangular prisms, pyramids and cylinders, and planes of symmetry in 3D shapes.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Use V = area of cross-section × length to find the volume of prisms and cylinders, and solve problems.

O2.t: Find the surface area of triangular prisms, pyramids and cylinders, using nets.

O3.t: Identify planes of symmetry in 3D shapes.

p: A farm has a cylindrical water tank **1.2 m across** and **1.5 m tall**, and a trough shaped like a **trapezium prism**.
How many litres does the tank hold? Is a cylinder a kind of prism? Think about it before you read on.
Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length.
A **prism** has the same cross-section all along its length: triangle, trapezium, hexagon … **V = A × l**.
Trapezium trough: parallel sides 0.5 m and 0.3 m, height 0.4 m, length 2 m → A = ½(0.5 + 0.3) × 0.4 = 0.16 m²; V = **0.32 m³ = 320 L**.
A **cylinder** is like a prism with a circular cross-section: **V = πr²h**.

qq.prompt: Cylinder r = 5 cm, h = 10 cm. Volume (cm³)? (1 d.p.)

lesson.t: How do I find the volume of a prism or cylinder?
p: Step 1: Identify the cross-section (it is the same all the way through).
Step 2: Find its area (circle πr², trapezium ½(a + b)h, triangle ½bh …).
Step 3: Multiply by the length or height.
Step 4: Use cubic units; convert to litres if needed (1000 cm³ = 1 L).

p: A food company makes a tin **8 cm tall** with radius **3 cm**. It needs a paper label all round the side, and metal for the top and bottom.
What shape is the label when you unroll it? How big is it? Think about it before you read on.
A net folds into a 3D shape; surface area = total area of the net.

qq.prompt: Square-based pyramid: base 6, triangle heights 5. Surface area?

p: Unroll the curved side: it becomes a **rectangle**. Its height is h and its length is the **circumference** 2πr.
Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles. Pyramid: base + triangular faces (use each triangle's slant height).
Sketch the net, label every face, and list areas so none is missed or counted twice.
Open shapes (no lid, a tube) have fewer faces – read the question carefully.

lesson.t: How do I find a surface area?
p: Step 1: Sketch the net and identify every face.
Step 2: Cylinder: two circles + a rectangle (2πr by h).
Step 3: Find each area; group identical faces.
Step 4: Add; give units squared; leave out missing faces for open shapes.

p: A rectangular cake (a cuboid, not a cube) must be cut by **one straight slice** into two halves that are exact mirror images.
How many different ways can you do it? Think about it before you read on.
A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry; a square has 4.

qq.prompt: Lines of symmetry of an equilateral triangle?

p: 3D shapes have **planes of symmetry**: a flat cut that splits the solid into two **congruent** halves that are mirror images.
A cuboid with three different edge lengths has **3** planes of symmetry (one parallel to each pair of faces) – so there are 3 ways to cut the cake.
Use isometric paper to draw solids and shade the plane of symmetry.
To check a plane: imagine a mirror on it – does each half reflect exactly onto the other?
Diagonal planes count too: a cube has 3 planes parallel to faces and 6 through opposite edges.

qq.prompt: Planes of symmetry of a square-based pyramid?
qq.hint: Two through the midpoints, two through the diagonals.

lesson.t: How do I find planes of symmetry?
p: Step 1: Look for cuts parallel to faces through the middle.
Step 2: Look for cuts through opposite edges or diagonals.
Step 3: Check each half is a mirror image of the other.
Step 4: Count carefully – don't count the same plane twice.

steps: one plane parallel to each pair of faces
diagonal planes don't work (faces aren't squares)

lesson.q: Prism with isosceles (not equilateral) triangle ends.

steps: any vertical plane through the apex

lesson.q: Planes of symmetry of a square-based cuboid 2 × 2 × 5.
lesson.why: The 4 vertical planes come from the square's 4 lines, but there is also a plane halfway along the length: 5.

lesson.t: Missing the plane across the length
p: Prisms also have a plane halfway along (if the ends are the same).
Car designers, architects and chemists use 3D symmetry; many molecules are symmetrical in planes.
A plane of symmetry cuts a solid into mirror-image halves.
Cuboid 3, square cuboid 5, cube 9.
Prism: lines of the end shape + 1.
Cylinders and cones: infinitely many.
